passage: In the small school near the paddy fields of Goa, Maria Miss closed the door after the prayer. "No lessons for ten minutes," she said. "I want to talk about words." She held up a crumpled sheet. "Once you crush paper, you can say sorry, but can you make it smooth again?" The class shook their heads. She did not say any name. But everyone knew about the story going around, and Dilnaz stared at her desk. After the bell, Maria Miss knelt by her. "If you want to talk, I'm here, or Sister Agnes in the office." At lunch, when someone whispered the story again, Dilnaz said clearly, "That isn't true." Her voice was steady, and the whisperer went quiet.

qa.q: What did Maria Miss hold up to the class?
qa.a: She held up a crumpled sheet of paper.

qa.q: How can you tell Dilnaz felt more confident by lunch?
qa.a: She said "That isn't true" clearly and with a steady voice, instead of staring at her desk like she did in the morning.

qa.q: What made Maria Miss's approach helpful?
qa.a: She talked about how words hurt without naming Dilnaz, so no one was embarrassed further, and then privately offered herself or Sister Agnes as someone to talk to.

qa.q: How might the whisperer see things after the class talk and Dilnaz's reply?
qa.a: They may feel caught and a little ashamed, realising the class now sees the story as hurtful and Dilnaz is not afraid of it.

grounding: It shows a teacher speaking to the class about hurtful words without naming the girl, offering her a trusted adult, and the girl calmly stating the truth.

passage: Outside the classroom window in Valencia, the orange trees swayed. Mr Santiago put down his marker. "Something has been going round this class," he said. "I'm not going to repeat it or say who it's about. But I want you to imagine hearing your name in a whisper, and not knowing what comes after it." Nobody spoke. Marek, the new boy, looked at his shoes. Later, as the class filed out, Mr Santiago quietly told Lucía, "The school counsellor, Ms Ortega, is very kind. Or you can talk to me anytime." Next morning, when a girl asked her in the corridor if the story was true, Lucía said, "No. It isn't." Just that. She walked on, and it felt better than hiding.

qa.q: What was swaying outside the classroom window?
qa.a: The orange trees were swaying outside the window.

qa.q: How did Lucía feel after answering the girl in the corridor?
qa.a: She felt stronger and relieved, because saying the truth simply felt better than hiding.

qa.q: How did Mr Santiago support Lucía without making things worse?
qa.a: He spoke to the whole class without naming her or repeating the story, then privately offered himself or Ms Ortega as people she could talk to.

qa.q: What might Marek have been thinking as he looked at his shoes?
qa.a: He may have felt guilty or uneasy, perhaps because he had heard or passed on the whisper himself.

grounding: It illustrates a teacher talking to the class about the hurt of whispers without naming the girl and pointing her to a trusted adult, so she learns to speak the truth calmly.

passage:
For a week, girls in Class 5 had whispered that Nikita still wet the bed. It wasn't true. Nikita now ate lunch alone.

On Monday, Vidya Ma'am closed the door and sat on her desk.

"I've heard some stories going around," she said. "I'm not going to say whose. But I want to talk about how words travel, and how they can hurt someone who sits right beside you."

Nobody looked at Nikita. Nikita looked at her desk.

After class, Vidya Ma'am asked Nikita to help carry books to the staffroom. On the way she said quietly, "If you ever want to talk, my door is open. And the counsellor, Mrs D'Souza, is kind."

Nikita nodded. The next day, when Rhea whispered something at lunch, Nikita said calmly, "That isn't true." Her voice didn't shake as much as she'd expected.

qa.q: Who is the counsellor Vidya Ma'am mentioned?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel when she said "That isn't true" the next day?
qa.a: She felt steadier and braver than expected, her voice hardly shaking, after having an adult's support.

qa.q: What made Vidya Ma'am's approach wise?
qa.a: She spoke to the class about hurtful words without naming Nikita, and then privately offered herself and the counsellor as trusted adults.

qa.q: How might the class have felt during Vidya Ma'am's talk?
qa.a: Some children, especially those who whispered, may have felt uncomfortable or guilty, recognising themselves.

grounding: Vidya Ma'am talks to the class about how words hurt without naming Nikita, offers her a trusted adult, and Nikita learns to say the truth calmly.

passage:
Rinki sits two benches in front of me, so I saw what happened.

Everyone was saying Rinki had copied her drawing from a book to win the prize. Rinki stopped raising her hand.

On Tuesday Mohit Sir, instead of starting maths, whispered a sentence to the first boy and asked him to pass it along the row. By the end, "Rinki drew a tiger" had become "Rinki got a tiger from a shop."

We all laughed. Then Mohit Sir said, "That is how stories change. And they can hurt real people."

He never said Rinki's name. Afterwards he talked to her by the window.

At lunch, when someone started again, Rinki said, "I drew it myself. You can watch me draw another." Nobody said anything after that.

— Kashish

qa.q: What had "Rinki drew a tiger" become by the end of the row?
qa.a: "Rinki got a tiger from a shop."

qa.q: How does Kashish seem to feel watching Rinki answer at lunch?
qa.a: Kashish seems impressed and a bit relieved, noticing how calmly Rinki stopped the story.

qa.q: What did Mohit Sir do that repaired the harm?
qa.a: He showed the class how stories change without naming Rinki, then spoke to her privately, giving her support to answer calmly.

qa.q: How might Rinki have felt when she said she drew it herself?
qa.a: She probably felt nervous but stronger, confident enough to speak the truth plainly after Mohit Sir's support.

grounding: Kashish observes Mohit Sir teaching the class how rumours twist without naming Rinki, supporting her privately, and Rinki answering calmly with the truth.

passage:
Monday. Nandini came to school to find a drawing on her desk: a girl with a runny nose and her name under it. People said she had lice. She didn't. She went home and cried.

Wednesday. Tanvir Sir noticed Nandini sitting alone at lunch. In the last period he talked to the class about how a joke can become a rumour and a rumour can feel like a wound. He didn't say Nandini's name. Afterwards he asked her to stay a minute and said, "You can come to me anytime. And Mrs Kaur in the office is kind to talk to."

Friday. When Arjit began to snigger again, Nandini looked straight at him and said, calmly, "That's not true. Please stop." He went red and stopped.

On the way home, Nandini realised her heart wasn't pounding at all.

qa.q: What was drawn on the paper left on Nandini's desk?
qa.a: A girl with a runny nose and her name under it.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel on Friday compared with Monday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt hurt and cried; by Friday she felt calm and steady enough to speak up.

qa.q: How did Tanvir Sir repair the harm?
qa.a: He talked to the whole class about how rumours hurt without naming Nandini, and privately offered himself and Mrs Kaur as trusted adults.

qa.q: How might Arjit feel when Nandini calmly says "Please stop"?
qa.a: He probably feels embarrassed and caught out, going red, since she answered without whispering or fighting.

grounding: Over a week Tanvir Sir talks to the class about hurtful words without naming Nandini, offers her trusted adults, and she learns to answer calmly.

passage: Worried about the whispering in your class, Uma? Let your old Elizabeth Aunty tell you about my Class 4, long ago. A story went round that little Sophia's father was in prison. It wasn't true, and she stopped eating her lunch. I didn't shout, and I didn't say her name. I asked the class, "Has anyone ever said something untrue about you? How did it feel?" Hands went up, one by one. Then I said, "Words can hurt like a push. If you hear a story about someone, bring it to me." At lunch I told Sophia quietly, "You can talk to me or to Mrs Rao any time." She came that same afternoon. The next week a boy stood up and said calmly, "That story is false." Nobody laughed at him.

qa.q: What story went round about Sophia?
qa.a: A story went round that Sophia's father was in prison.

qa.q: How was Sophia feeling when she stopped eating her lunch?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and ashamed by the false story, too upset to eat.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make with the class, and why did it help?
qa.a: She talked about how words hurt without naming Sophia, so nobody was shamed, and gave the children and Sophia a trusted adult to go to.

qa.q: What might the boy have felt when he stood up and said, 'That story is false'?
qa.a: He may have felt nervous but brave, and then steadier when nobody laughed at him for saying the truth calmly.

grounding: Shows a teacher addressing a rumour with the class without naming the girl, offering her a trusted adult, and a child learning that calm truth beats whispering.
